text:
Africa’s electricity-access push is accelerating. The harder question is what happens after the connection.

Mission 300 reported in June 2026 that more than 50 million people had already gained electricity access through aligned programmes across 40 countries.

But more than 560 million people in sub-Saharan Africa still lacked electricity in the latest Tracking SDG 7 assessment. As programmes move deeper into rural, remote and lower-income markets, the economics of every new connection become harder.

StoneComms’ finding is that productive demand can be part of the solution.

A household connection is valuable in its own right. But a farm pump, cold room, clinic, school, workshop, water system or charging hub can also become an anchor load that improves utilisation of the energy asset serving everyone around it.

IEA analysis finds that businesses connected to mini-grids consume nearly three times as much electricity per connection as households. Public institutions can consume around six times as much.

That changes the financing logic. A mini-grid with weak daytime demand still carries most of its capital and operating costs. A productive customer can use spare capacity, improve the load shape and strengthen revenue — provided the local economy can support the activity.

Ethiopia’s DREAM programme links renewable mini-grids to agricultural demand. Nigeria’s DARES programme includes productive-use equipment and Solar for Business. Regional DARES in West and Central Africa combines distributed renewables, results-based finance and productive-use objectives.

StoneComms proposes a Load Activation Covenant for distributed-energy finance.

Where public or development capital supports a distributed-energy asset, the financing package should define not only how many connections will be made, but how useful demand will be activated around them.

That means:

Map the load before finalising the asset.
Finance the appliance, not only the wire.
Secure credible anchor demand where the model needs it.
Report productive kilowatt-hours alongside connection counts.
Define a route away from subsidy as utilisation strengthens.

This is not an argument to turn every electricity project into an SME programme. Productive-use equipment can waste money where roads, water, markets, skills or working capital are the real constraint. The point is to test demand as rigorously as supply.

For governments, DFIs, developers and investors, the next question is not only “how many people did we connect?” It is “what economic and social capacity did those connections leave switched on?”
